title: Tech deep dive: Auto-rollback on SLO breach (latency/error) + auditability
next_steps: Redwood to share draft policy defaults (min traffic, warm-up delay, cooldown, baseline compare) used for auto-rollback and what is configurable per tenant/route.
HelioBank to send their current SLO targets (p95/p99 latency and 5xx budget) for two critical routes and whether they prefer burn-rate style or fixed threshold.
Redwood to share sample audit event payloads for: policy change, automated rollback trigger, rollback executor action, and manual override/ack (for SIEM review).
Schedule a follow-up with HelioBank SRE to walk through monitor identity/label contract and a dry-run (synthetic breach) plan.
transcript:
Fireflies.ai Transcript

Meeting: Tech deep dive: Auto-rollback on SLO breach (latency/error) + auditability
Date: 2025-01-23
Start time: 10:00 AM PT
Duration: 57 min
Recorded by: Fireflies.ai

Attendees
- Redwood Inference: Dylan Brooks, Ethan Park, Benji Okafor, Allison Grant, Naomi Feldman
- HelioBank: Priya Desai, Mark Feldman, Jin Park, Olivia Chen, Samir Qureshi

---

Summary (auto-generated)
HelioBank asked for details on Redwood’s upcoming auto-rollback capability tied to latency and error-rate SLOs. Discussion covered how monitors are identified (labels/identity contract), evaluation semantics (windows, minimum traffic, warm-up, cooldown, baseline comparisons, and burn-rate vs fixed thresholds), behavior during monitoring outages (unknown verdict, fail-open/closed), and auditability (event types, who initiated, and SIEM export). Redwood walked through guardrails to prevent rollback flapping and cascading rollbacks across many tenants.

Topics (auto-generated)
- Rollout + canary traffic split rollback behavior
- SLO definitions (latency + 5xx) and evaluation windows
- Monitor identity contract: route/model/region/tier labels
- Baseline comparison and warm-up guards
- Monitor staleness and “unknown” verdict
- Audit events, RBAC, and compliance needs

Action items (auto-generated)
- Dylan Brooks: send sample audit log events + SIEM export notes (by next week)
- Allison Grant: share monitor label/identity examples for route/model/region/tier (by Friday)
- Ethan Park: confirm rate limiting approach for simultaneous rollbacks (by next sync)
- HelioBank (Mark): provide current SLO thresholds and windowing preferences (by Monday)

---

[00:00] Dylan Brooks: Alright, cool. Uh, thanks everybody for joining. This is Dylan from Redwood. We pulled Ethan and Benji from the control plane team, Allison from observability standards, and Naomi from compliance. The goal today is to go deep on the auto-rollback-on-SLO-breach thing you asked about. Priya, do you want to frame what you’re trying to solve?

[00:23] Priya Desai: Yeah. Thanks Dylan. So, we’ve had a couple incidents where a model rollout increases tail latency. Like p99 goes sideways. We have canaries, we have monitors, but the rollback is manual and too slow. We want… ideally… if latency or 5xx breaches, revert traffic automatically. But we need it to be safe. No flapping. And we need audit logs, like, what triggered it, what it changed, and who can override.

[00:49] Mark Feldman: And, we’re in finance. So if this is “automation that changes prod behavior,” we need to see the evidence and control. Also we do not want a situation where monitoring is broken and then it rolls back everything. That’s… yeah.

[01:04] Dylan Brooks: Yup. Makes sense. Ethan, do you want to give a 60-second overview of how we’re thinking about it?

[01:10] Ethan Park: Sure. So today the rollout controller already manages traffic splits for canary and A/B, per route. The new piece is an SLO evaluator module. It pulls standardized monitors—latency and error—based on a canonical “monitor identity” (labels like route, model, version, region, tier). It evaluates policy thresholds over windows, with guardrails: minimum traffic, warm-up delay, cooldown, and optionally “must be worse than baseline.” If it’s a breach, it triggers rollback executor to revert split to last stable and emits events (audit + notification).

[01:45] Samir Qureshi: When you say “monitors,” are we talking like Datadog monitors? Or Prometheus alert rules? Or your own thing?

[01:52] Allison Grant: Good question. We’re not building a new monitoring product. We rely on our existing telemetry pipeline and our SLO tooling. Under the hood, the metrics live in our metrics store; dashboards are in Grafana for most tenants, and we also integrate to Datadog in some environments. The key is: the rollout controller doesn’t hardcode a vendor. It calls our monitoring API with a monitor identity and gets back computed time series / SLO burn info.

[02:19] Jin Park: So there is a monitoring API between controller and metrics store.

[02:23] Benji Okafor: Yeah. Internally we call it the “SLO monitor service.” It has query templates and it can return “current value,” “window stats,” and “freshness.”

[02:32] Mark Feldman: Can we talk about the SLO definitions? Like what exactly are you measuring for “latency”? p95? p99? Mean? And what’s the denominator for errors?

[02:43] Allison Grant: For rollback decisions we keep it intentionally constrained. Latency SLO is usually p95 or p99 of end-to-end request latency at the API gateway for a specific route. Default is p95 for Hosted, and p99 for Dedicated tends to be what SRE teams care about, but it’s configurable. Errors is typically 5xx rate over total requests for that same route.

[03:07] Mark Feldman: Is it per region? Because we see region-specific issues.

[03:10] Allison Grant: Yes—region is one of the canonical dimensions. The monitor identity includes region so you can roll back in, say, us-east without automatically rolling back eu-west.

[03:22] Priya Desai: That’s key. We don’t want global changes from a single region blip.

[03:26] Ethan Park: Right, and the rollback action is scoped the same way as the rollout config. If you’re doing a regional rollout, it rolls back that region’s traffic split.

[03:36] Samir Qureshi: What about tenant? We have multiple internal business units; you might call it “customer tier.”

[03:42] Benji Okafor: In our system it’s tenant + tier. For enterprise we often have “dedicated” tier vs “hosted shared.” The monitor identity supports “customer_tier” and “tenant_id.” We also have guardrails so one tenant’s rollback doesn’t cascade into others.

[03:58] Mark Feldman: Okay. Now semantics. Like, if p99 breaches for 2 minutes, do you roll back? That would be… noisy.

[04:08] Ethan Park: That’s the core of it. We have policy semantics that are configurable. Conceptually: you specify the metric, threshold, evaluation window, and a trigger condition like “breach for N of M datapoints” or “burn rate above X.” We’re leaning toward windows like 5 minutes short window and 30 minutes long window, and requiring both to be bad (or a stronger condition on short window), plus a minimum request count.

[04:35] Jin Park: Burn rate like SRE burn rate? 14x, 6x, whatever.

[04:39] Ethan Park: Yeah, similar idea. Though in our rollout case we often don’t have a full monthly error budget for a canary. So we support both: burn rate style if you define an SLO target (like 99.9) and thresholds style if you prefer “p99 < 900ms.”

[04:58] Mark Feldman: We’d probably prefer fixed thresholds for latency. For error we can do budget. But… depends.

[05:05] Allison Grant: We see that a lot. Latency thresholds are more intuitive.

[05:09] Priya Desai: What about “baseline comparison”? Like we want “must be worse than stable,” not just “above 900ms” because sometimes stable is already 880 and then you’ll roll back for normal noise.

[05:23] Benji Okafor: Yep. There’s an option: “must_be_worse_than_baseline.” Baseline is typically the prior stable version’s metric over the same window, with some margin. So you can say: rollback only if canary p99 > max(threshold, baseline * 1.15). Or baseline + absolute delta.

[05:44] Samir Qureshi: That’s good. But how do you compute baseline if stable and canary share infra? Like, if there’s a regional GPU shortage, both get worse.

[05:53] Ethan Park: Exactly. That’s why baseline compare is optional, and we also have “incident correlation” concerns. The safe default we’re considering is: require absolute threshold breach AND optional baseline condition. In addition, we have a “global incident” flag from SRE that can suppress auto rollbacks if the whole region is degraded.

[06:14] Mark Feldman: Wait, “global incident flag” as in you manually set it?

[06:18] Ethan Park: Yeah, basically an operator override: “pause automation for this scope.” We can integrate it with incident management tooling, but at minimum it’s a manual toggle.

[06:30] Dylan Brooks: Priya, Mark, is that aligned with how you’d want to run it? Like a big red button “pause rollbacks.”

[06:36] Mark Feldman: Yes. We need a “hold.” Because if monitors go crazy during an upstream outage, we don’t want it to thrash.

[06:44] Naomi Feldman: From compliance standpoint, that “pause” and any manual override actions need to be audited. Who paused it, when, and for what scope.

[06:53] Olivia Chen: Yeah. Also need RBAC. Like only SRE on-call can pause automation or acknowledge.

[07:00] Naomi Feldman: Exactly.

[07:03] Jin Park: Can we get into “monitor identity contract”? Like what labels are required and how do you avoid cardinality explosion? Because we’ve had issues with “model_version” as a label.

[07:15] Allison Grant: Sure. So the identity is basically a set of tags: service (rollout-controller managed route), route_id, model_id, model_version, region, and tier. For the monitors used by automation, we constrain it so it’s not “free-form.” It’s enumerated in config. Also, we normalize model version to a short stable identifier rather than a full git sha.

[07:38] Benji Okafor: And we don’t create monitors per prompt or per customer end-user. It’s per tenant/route/model/version/region/tier. Still high, but manageable.

[07:49] Mark Feldman: So, if we have 20 routes and multiple model versions, this is still… a lot.

[07:55] Allison Grant: Totally. That’s why query templates matter. We generate monitors programmatically and we enforce label presence. Also, for rollouts, you typically only have two versions active: stable and candidate. The number of “live identities” is bounded.

[08:11] Samir Qureshi: How do you handle shadow traffic? Like we send 1% shadow to candidate but not serving result. Should that trigger rollback?

[08:19] Ethan Park: No, we separate shadow evaluation. Auto-rollback triggers only on serving traffic split changes. Shadow routes are excluded from rollback policy, because they can see different latency characteristics and it could false trigger.

[08:35] Priya Desai: What about warm-up? Like, when a new model spins up, first few minutes are slower.

[08:41] Benji Okafor: We have a “warm_up” or “grace period” after a rollout step. Policy can say: don’t evaluate for X minutes after traffic changes or after model becomes “ready.” Also we can require minimum request volume, like at least 300 requests in the evaluation window.

[09:01] Mark Feldman: Minimum traffic is mandatory in our view. Otherwise low traffic route will flap.

[09:06] Ethan Park: Agreed. We’re shipping minimum traffic as default guardrail.

[09:10] Jin Park: And cooldown? Once it rolls back, do you lock out further actions?

[09:16] Benji Okafor: Yes. Cooldown period prevents repeated rollbacks. Also we use idempotency keys so if multiple evaluator loops see the same breach, executor only acts once.

[09:28] Priya Desai: So it rolls back to prior stable version. How do you define “stable”? Like what if stable is not actually stable, or stable has drifted.

[09:38] Ethan Park: In the rollout controller, stable is the last version that was marked “promoted” for that route. We keep an explicit pointer: current_candidate and current_stable. Rollback means revert traffic weights to 100% stable, 0% candidate, and optionally freeze the rollout.

[09:56] Dylan Brooks: And you can require manual ack to resume, depending on policy.

[10:02] Mark Feldman: That’s important. After rollback, we want the system to stop trying to progress.

[10:06] Ethan Park: Exactly.

[10:08] Olivia Chen: On audit logs: what is included? We need to export to Splunk. We need “what changed” and “why.”

[10:16] Naomi Feldman: Our audit event schema includes: actor (system vs user), actor_id, tenant, scope (route/model/version/region), policy version, trigger reason (which SLO, threshold, observed values), and the action (traffic split before/after). For automated triggers, actor is “rollout-controller” with a service identity, but we also include the on-call escalation channel it notified.

[10:39] Olivia Chen: Do you include raw metric points?

[10:42] Naomi Feldman: Not raw timeseries in the audit event, typically. But we include summary: window start/end, computed p99, error rate, request count, and links to the dashboard panel with those queries.

[10:56] Jin Park: Links are fine. Forensics can pull from Grafana.

[11:00] Mark Feldman: What about “monitor outage” case. Like metrics pipeline delayed. What does the evaluator do?

[11:06] Benji Okafor: We introduced an explicit “unknown verdict.” If monitor data is stale or missing, we do not treat it as a breach. We classify the verdict as unknown, emit an internal metric “monitor_fetch_errors,” and optionally page if it persists.

[11:24] Mark Feldman: That’s fail-open, right? It won’t rollback.

[11:27] Ethan Park: Correct. Default is fail-open for automation because fail-closed could cause massive rollbacks due to monitoring outages. But the policy can be configured. Some customers prefer fail-closed for certain critical routes, but it’s risky.

[11:44] Priya Desai: We probably want fail-open, but with alerting that the automation is blind.

[11:49] Allison Grant: Exactly. We have a separate alert: “SLO evaluator blind / data stale.” That should page SRE but not rollback.

[11:58] Samir Qureshi: What counts as stale? Like 2 minutes? 10 minutes?

[12:03] Benji Okafor: Configurable. Defaults we’re discussing are something like: datapoint freshness within 2x scrape interval, but in practice we say if the last timestamp is older than 3 minutes for 1m resolution queries, we mark as stale. Again, depends on backend.

[12:20] Jin Park: We’ve seen metric delays in batch pipelines. But you’re using near-real-time counters at the edge, right?

[12:26] Allison Grant: For rollback signals we only use near-real-time signals, yes. We avoid derived analytics that lag.

[12:34] Mark Feldman: Great. Now, “false positives” concern: correlated incidents. Like upstream network. How do you avoid rolling back a model when the real issue is something else?

[12:45] Ethan Park: You can’t fully solve that, but guardrails help. Baseline compare helps (if both stable and canary degrade, you don’t rollback if requirement is “worse than baseline”). Another guardrail is requiring the breach to be specific to the candidate. For example, we can compare error codes: if 5xx are from upstream dependency timeouts across both, not candidate-specific. But that’s more advanced.

[13:10] Benji Okafor: Also, rollback is not always harmful, but it can be. We’re adding rate limits: per tenant and global. So if many routes breach simultaneously due to region incident, it won’t roll back everything at once.

[13:25] Mark Feldman: Rate limit is huge. We’ve had automation stampede problems.

[13:29] Ethan Park: Right. Think “max rollbacks per tenant per 10 minutes” plus a global ceiling. If ceiling is hit, we pause and page.

[13:42] Priya Desai: How does it notify? Slack? PagerDuty?

[13:46] Dylan Brooks: Today, Slack for most customers, and we integrate to incident bot. For enterprise, we can post to your on-call channel with links to the rollout page + dashboards + runbook.

[13:58] Jin Park: Do you have an API event stream? We would like to ingest into our tooling.

[14:03] Naomi Feldman: Yes, audit events can be streamed to your SIEM via export integration. For near-real-time, we also have an event stream (webhook) for “rollback_triggered.”

[14:15] Olivia Chen: Webhook needs signing and allowlist.

[14:18] Naomi Feldman: Yup, HMAC signing, and we can restrict by IPs; for private deployments it stays inside your network.

[14:28] Samir Qureshi: Speaking of private deployment… we run in our VPC. Does the monitor service run in our VPC too?

[14:35] Ethan Park: For Redwood Private, yes—control plane and the monitor query service can be deployed in your VPC depending on architecture. We can also integrate with your existing Prometheus if needed, but the simplest is using our packaged observability stack.

[14:53] Mark Feldman: We might prefer to use our Prometheus/Grafana rather than yours. But we can talk later.

[15:00] Allison Grant: We’ve done both. The key requirement is consistent label mapping and query templates.

[15:07] Priya Desai: Can we walk through a concrete example? Like p99 latency threshold 900ms, window 5 minutes, minimum 500 requests, cooldown 30 minutes, warm-up 10 minutes. How would it decide?

[15:21] Benji Okafor: Sure. So: rollout step shifts from 0% to 10% canary. That emits a “rollout_step_changed” event. Evaluator sets a grace period timer, say 10 minutes. After grace, each evaluation tick (like every 60 seconds), it queries the monitor for canary scope: route A, candidate v2, us-east, tier dedicated. It gets p99 for last 5 minutes and request count. If requests >= 500 and p99 > 900ms for, say, 3 consecutive ticks, then it’s a breach. If baseline compare is enabled, it also fetches stable p99 and checks canary > baseline * 1.15.

[16:00] Benji Okafor: If breach true, it emits “auto_rollback_triggered” audit event with the metric snapshot, then calls executor to update traffic split to stable. Executor writes config change with an idempotency key like tenant/route/candidate/version and timestamp window. Then it emits “auto_rollback_executed.”

[16:22] Priya Desai: Nice. And then it stops rollout.

[16:25] Ethan Park: Yes. Rollout state becomes “paused_due_to_health.”

[16:29] Mark Feldman: Can the operator resume, or does it require a new rollout?

[16:34] Ethan Park: Operator can resume after acknowledging. It depends on policy. Some want “manual ack required.”

[16:43] Olivia Chen: Acknowledgement event should be audited.

[16:46] Naomi Feldman: It is.

[16:49] Jin Park: How do you represent these policies? Like YAML? UI? API?

[16:55] Dylan Brooks: Both. In Console you can set a policy per route, and there’s an API/CRD style config for automation teams.

[17:04] Priya Desai: We’ll want config-as-code.

[17:06] Ethan Park: That’s supported. The schema allows per route/model/region/tier overrides, plus defaults.

[17:16] Mark Feldman: Any gotchas with cardinality if you do per region and per tier and per route?

[17:21] Allison Grant: It’s manageable because it’s still “rollout-scoped.” But yes we enforce constraints and have linting. If someone tries to define a policy on “customer_id = *” across all tenants, we reject.

[17:37] Samir Qureshi: That’s good. Another question: do you evaluate on absolute latency, or can you evaluate on “delta relative to baseline”? That’s sometimes better.

[17:47] Ethan Park: We support both styles. The “must be worse than baseline” is essentially delta. You can set it as ratio or absolute. For example, “candidate p99 > baseline p99 + 150ms.”

[18:02] Jin Park: And you can still have an absolute cap, like “never exceed 2 seconds.”

[18:06] Benji Okafor: Exactly.

[18:09] Mark Feldman: We also care about error rate spikes. Sometimes latency is ok but 503 spikes under load.

[18:15] Allison Grant: Error SLO is typically 5xx/total. We also have exclusion lists (e.g., client cancellations, 499) depending on gateway semantics. For rollback we focus on server errors.

[18:30] Mark Feldman: Do you distinguish 502 due to upstream vs 500 from model server.

[18:34] Allison Grant: We can, if those labels are available. For the first version, we’re using top-level 5xx. But we can add “error_class” breakdown in dashboards.

[18:46] Priya Desai: If you rollback due to error spike, will it necessarily fix it? Like if the candidate is causing it, yes. But if it’s infra, no.

[18:54] Ethan Park: Right. Rollback is best-effort mitigation. It reduces MTTR when the candidate is the culprit. If not, at least it stabilizes config and gives you signal.

[19:07] Dylan Brooks: On the business side, we see customers want “less time to revert a bad deploy.” That’s the core.

[19:14] Jin Park: How quickly can it detect? Like what’s the loop time.

[19:18] Benji Okafor: In our prototype, evaluation every 60 seconds, with a 5-minute window. So earliest detection is ~5-6 minutes after grace ends. But you can do 2-minute windows if your metrics are stable.

[19:35] Mark Feldman: We’d like faster, but we also know shorter windows are noisy.

[19:40] Allison Grant: Exactly. That’s why we often do “short window + long window.”

[19:45] Priya Desai: So if short window is bad but long window not yet bad, you hold.

[19:49] Ethan Park: Right. Or you can set a “critical threshold” that triggers on short window alone (like p99 > 3 seconds) to catch catastrophic regressions.

[20:04] Mark Feldman: That’s good.

[20:06] Olivia Chen: On audit and retention: How long do you retain audit logs? We need minimum one year.

[20:13] Naomi Feldman: For enterprise, we offer extended retention. Default is 90 days in Console, but you can export continuously to your SIEM for longer. For Private deployments, retention is controlled by you.

[20:28] Olivia Chen: And access control? Can developers see rollback history?

[20:33] Naomi Feldman: RBAC-based. You can allow read-only for devs and restrict override controls to SRE.

[20:41] Priya Desai: Great.

[20:43] Samir Qureshi: Switching gears: what if the rollout itself is multi-step, like 10%, 25%, 50%, 100%. Does the policy apply at each step?

[20:53] Ethan Park: Yes. Each step change resets grace period, and evaluation continues. If it breaches at 25%, it rolls back to stable.

[21:05] Jin Park: Does it ever roll back to previous step, like from 50% to 25%?

[21:10] Ethan Park: In the initial version, rollback is to stable (last promoted). Partial rollback can be confusing. But we’ve discussed “step-down” as a future enhancement.

[21:22] Mark Feldman: Stable rollback is fine.

[21:24] Dylan Brooks: Another thing you asked in email was “who initiated.” For automation it’s system, but we log the policy that allowed it.

[21:31] Olivia Chen: Right. And policy changes need approval workflow maybe.

[21:36] Naomi Feldman: We can integrate with change management via config-as-code reviews. In Console, policy changes are audited with user, timestamp, diff summary.

[21:50] Priya Desai: Good.

[21:52] Mark Feldman: Edge case: what if stable is older and has a security patch missing. We might not want to roll back.

[22:00] Ethan Park: That’s a tricky one. Policy can allow “disable auto rollback” for that route, or set “manual approval required for rollback.” Another pattern is “fallback version list” where stable is not one version but a set of allowed fallbacks.

[22:17] Benji Okafor: Today it’s basically stable pointer. But we can support allowlist. We’ve heard this from regulated customers.

[22:25] Priya Desai: We would likely use manual for those.

[22:28] Jin Park: Another edge: if stable is also unhealthy, you might roll back and still be in breach.

[22:35] Allison Grant: That’s where baseline compare becomes tricky. The dashboard will show both. Rollback may not help but it stops pushing a risky version.

[22:47] Mark Feldman: Okay.

[22:48] Dylan Brooks: Can I check: are you using Datadog today for SLOs?

[22:52] Mark Feldman: Mix. We use Datadog for infra and some service metrics, Grafana for app metrics. And PagerDuty.

[23:00] Dylan Brooks: Got it. We can align with that.

[23:03] Samir Qureshi: I want to understand data path: request comes in, you emit latency histograms, those get labeled by route and model version. Then monitor queries compute p99.

[23:15] Allison Grant: Yes. There’s an important point: model version label must be set consistently at the ingress, not only at the model server. Otherwise you can’t compute route-level p99 per version.

[23:28] Jin Park: We’ve had label drift issues. Like sometimes “region” is “use1” vs “us-east-1.”

[23:34] Allison Grant: Exactly. That’s why the identity contract includes normalization. We’re doing migration to standard values.

[23:45] Mark Feldman: Are you planning to enforce that? Like if missing labels, does rollout automation refuse to enable?

[23:52] Benji Okafor: Yes. The evaluator will surface “monitor invalid/missing labels” and keep verdict unknown. And we can block enabling auto-rollback on a route until monitors validate.

[24:07] Priya Desai: That’s good. Make it hard to misconfigure.

[24:11] Ethan Park: We also expose “decision trace” logs—basically why it decided breach/no-breach/unknown.

[24:20] Jin Park: That’s huge for debugging.

[24:24] Mark Feldman: And can we see it in Console?

[24:26] Dylan Brooks: That’s the plan, yes. Health verdict with the last evaluation details.

[24:33] Olivia Chen: One more on security: if this is in our VPC, does Redwood staff have access to trigger rollbacks?

[24:40] Naomi Feldman: In Private, you control access. Redwood does not have standing access. Support access is time-bound and requires your approval (break-glass). Actions are audited.

[24:55] Olivia Chen: Great.

[24:57] (crosstalk)

[25:00] Priya Desai: Let’s talk thresholds. Do you have recommended defaults for enterprise? We don’t want to spend weeks tuning.

[25:08] Allison Grant: We can propose defaults based on tier. Example: warm-up 10 minutes after traffic shift; minimum 200 requests in 5 minutes; latency threshold set to your SLO target plus buffer; error threshold maybe 1% 5xx for 5 min and 0.5% for 30 min. Cooldown 30 minutes. Baseline compare on with 15% margin.

[25:34] Mark Feldman: Those seem plausible but we’d want to align with our own SLOs.

[25:39] Dylan Brooks: If you send us your current SLO docs for the two critical routes, we’ll map.

[25:45] Jin Park: Does the evaluator account for canary traffic being lower, so percent calculations are noisy?

[25:52] Benji Okafor: Yes. That’s why minimum request count is important. Also we can use Wilson interval style guardrails, but that’s probably v2. For v1 it’s min traffic + windowing.

[26:10] Mark Feldman: Another concern: if canary is 1% traffic, it might not hit min requests. So you’ll never rollback.

[26:17] Ethan Park: True. We recommend canary size that gives enough samples to evaluate. Or you can use longer windows. Another option is a “critical threshold” that triggers even with lower traffic if it’s catastrophic.

[26:33] Priya Desai: Makes sense.

[26:35] Samir Qureshi: Do you support “per route” policies? Because we have some routes that are batch jobs, latency can be high, but errors matter.

[26:44] Ethan Park: Yes, per route. You can have different monitors and thresholds.

[26:49] Mark Feldman: Okay.

[26:50] Dylan Brooks: We’ve got about 25 minutes left. Anything else you want to drill into?

[26:56] Olivia Chen: I want a concrete example of audit event payload, even if redacted.

[27:02] Naomi Feldman: Yep. We can send a sample. It’ll look like: event_type=rollout.auto_rollback.triggered, actor=system, scope={tenant, route, region, candidate_version}, reason={metric: latency_p99, window: 5m, observed: 1.42s, threshold: 0.9s, baseline: 0.88s, request_count: 1240}, policy_id and policy_revision, plus links.

[27:28] Olivia Chen: Perfect.

[27:30] Jin Park: I want to understand what happens if the rollback executor fails. Like config update fails due to lock.

[27:37] Benji Okafor: Executor is retried with backoff. It’s idempotent. If it can’t apply change, it emits an “execution_failed” event and pages. But it won’t keep thrashing.

[27:52] Ethan Park: Also, the evaluator and executor are decoupled. Evaluator makes a decision, stores it, executor acts. So if executor is down, the decision is preserved.

[28:07] Mark Feldman: Where is that stored?

[28:09] Benji Okafor: In our control plane DB (rollout state store). For Private it’s your DB.

[28:16] Jin Park: Great.

[28:18] Priya Desai: Another thing: do you have “manual rollback” button in Console and does it use same executor path?

[28:26] Dylan Brooks: Yes, and it uses the same executor, which means same audit events.

[28:32] Naomi Feldman: Manual rollback is event_type=rollout.rollback.manual, actor=user.

[28:39] Mark Feldman: Perfect.

[28:41] Samir Qureshi: Slight tangent: do you also rollback on quality regressions? Like eval scores.

[28:47] Dylan Brooks: Not in this project. This is latency and error only. Quality gates are separate pipeline.

[28:53] Priya Desai: Ok.

[28:54] Mark Feldman: How do you prevent “cascading rollbacks across many tenants”? You mentioned global rate limit.

[29:01] Ethan Park: We do two things. One: per-tenant max rollbacks. Two: global max rollbacks in a time window, plus a “blast radius” check. If a single monitor backend is returning errors for everyone, we stop automation and raise an incident.

[29:18] Jin Park: Nice.

[29:20] Allison Grant: And we monitor the automation itself: evaluator lag, monitor fetch error rate, number of unknown verdicts.
